newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Global nature talks end in Argentina, aim met.
newsitem.headline: Global nature talks end in Argentina, aim met.

text.p: Delegates to a conference on biological diversity claimed on Friday to have made headway in world conservation efforts but environmentalists said progress was minimal and governments blocked significant proposals.

Organisers of the two-week Third Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biodiversity said at Friday's close that the meeting fulfilled its original aim of steering nations toward the development of national action plans.
"It was a big leap forward. We made progress even where we didn't really expect to achieve anything significant," Calestous Juma, exective-secretary of the convention told Reuters.
The conference agreed to hold a special workshop late next year on indigenous rights and to work closely with the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) to influence its decisions.
Governments from 162 nations also agreed to draft a global forest protection programme by their next meeting in March 1998.

"It would have been a utopia to launch a programme now, even though Argentina favoured that. But we spoke about forests for the first time in this conference, which is very significant," said Carlos Merenson, head of the Argentine delegation.

The conference also signed a memorandum of understanding that allows the convention to set priorities for financing by the Global Environment Facility, a fund managed by the World Bank and United Nations agencies.

The GEF board, which so far has allocated funds itself, will review the request in coming months. Bickering over control of funds prevented the conference from appointing the GEF as the permanent financing mechanism.
Environmental groups argued the meeting failed to take any urgent action to prevent further loss of ecosystems as required by the Convention on Biodiversity, drafted at the 1992 Earth Summit.
The United States, Canada and Brazil blocked agreement on various plans sponsored by the European Union and others, for immediate action to protect the world's forests.

The Geneva-based World Wide Fund for Nature decried the lack of a concrete protection programme for forests, which contain 70 percent of the world's land biodiversity and were being depleted at an alarming rate of 74 acres (30 hectares) per minute.
